title: Control Flow
description: Direct your program's logic with conditionals and loops

lessons.title: if, elif, else
lessons.description: Make decisions in your code with conditionals

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Write if/elif/else chains and understand Python's indentation-based blocks.

sections.title: 🔀 Basic Conditionals
sections.content:
Python uses indentation (not braces) to define blocks.

```python
age = 20

if age >= 18:
    print("Adult")
elif age >= 13:
    print("Teenager")
else:
    print("Child")
```

Only one branch runs — Python checks each condition top to bottom and stops at the first True one.

sections.title: 🧩 Nested & Combined Conditions
Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting the colon `:` after the condition, or mixing tabs and spaces for indentation (Python will error).

questions.question: What defines a code block in Python?
questions.explanation: Python uses consistent indentation instead of braces.

questions.question: How many branches of an if/elif/else run?
questions.explanation: Python stops at the first True condition and skips the rest.

questions.question: What must follow an if condition?
questions.explanation: The colon starts the indented block.

questions.question: `elif` is short for...
questions.explanation: elif lets you check another condition without full nesting.

questions.question: If no condition is True and there's no else, what happens?
questions.explanation: If nothing matches and there's no else, the if statement simply does nothing.

questions.question: Mixing tabs and spaces in Python...
questions.explanation: Python needs consistent whitespace for blocks.

questions.question: Which condition style is generally preferred?
questions.explanation: Combined conditions are often more readable than deep nesting.

questions.question: What type must an if condition evaluate to (or be treated as)?
questions.explanation: if evaluates the condition's truthiness.

lessons.title: Comparison & Logical Operators in Conditions
lessons.description: Build richer conditions by combining comparisons

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Chain comparisons and combine them with and/or/not confidently.

sections.title: 🔗 Chaining Comparisons
sections.content:
Python allows elegant chained comparisons.

```python
age = 25
18 <= age <= 65   # True, same as (18 <= age) and (age <= 65)
```

sections.title: 🧠 Combining with Logic
sections.content:
```python
username = "admin"
password = "1234"

if username == "admin" and password == "1234":
    print("Access granted")

if username == "admin" or username == "root":
    print("Privileged user")
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Writing `if 18 <= age and age <= 65` when `18 <= age <= 65` is cleaner and equally valid.

questions.question: What does `18 <= age <= 65` mean?
questions.explanation: Python supports chained comparisons directly.

questions.question: `True and False` evaluates to...
questions.explanation: and requires both sides to be True.

questions.question: `False or True` evaluates to...
questions.explanation: or is True if at least one side is True.

questions.question: What does `not (5 > 3)` return?
questions.explanation: 5 > 3 is True, so not flips it to False.

questions.question: Operator precedence: `not` binds...
questions.explanation: not applies before and/or in an expression.

questions.question: `5 == 5 and 3 != 3` is...
questions.explanation: 3 != 3 is False, so the whole and is False.

questions.question: Chained comparisons like `a < b < c` are equivalent to...
questions.explanation: Python evaluates each adjacent pair and ANDs them together.

questions.question: Which combines two conditions requiring both true?
questions.explanation: and requires both operands to be True.

lessons.title: while Loops
lessons.description: Repeat code while a condition stays true

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Write while loops, avoid infinite loops, and use them for unknown-length repetition.

sections.title: 🔁 Basic while Loop
sections.content:
A while loop repeats as long as its condition is True.

```python
count = 0
while count < 5:
    print(count)
    count += 1   # crucial! must eventually make condition False
```

sections.title: ♾️ Infinite Loops & break
sections.content:
Sometimes you loop 'forever' until something inside tells you to stop.

```python
while True:
    answer = input("Type 'quit' to stop: ")
    if answer == "quit":
        break
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting to update the loop variable, causing an infinite loop that never becomes False.

questions.question: A while loop keeps running as long as...
questions.explanation: The loop re-checks the condition each iteration.

questions.question: What commonly causes an infinite loop?
options: Forgetting to update the loop variable
questions.explanation: If the condition never becomes False, the loop never ends.

questions.question: What does `break` do inside a loop?
questions.explanation: break exits the nearest enclosing loop immediately.

questions.question: `while True:` combined with a conditional break is used for...
options: Loops with an unclear number of iterations
questions.explanation: It's a common pattern for 'loop until some condition happens'.

questions.question: How many times does `while False:` run its body?
questions.explanation: The condition is checked before the first iteration.

questions.question: What's essential to avoid an infinite while loop?
options: Something in the loop must change the condition
questions.explanation: The condition must eventually evaluate to False.

questions.question: Where is a while loop most useful compared to a for loop?
options: When the number of iterations isn't known in advance
questions.explanation: while shines when you don't know ahead of time how many iterations you need.

questions.question: What happens right after `break` executes?
options: Control jumps to the code right after the loop
questions.explanation: break exits the loop but the rest of the program continues.

lessons.title: for Loops & range()
lessons.description: Iterate over sequences and generate number ranges

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Loop over strings, lists, and ranges with for.

sections.title: 🔁 for Loops
sections.content:
A for loop iterates directly over the items of a sequence.

```python
for letter in "abc":
    print(letter)   # a, b, c

for fruit in ["apple", "banana"]:
    print(fruit)
```

sections.title: 🔢 range()
sections.content:
range() generates a sequence of numbers, commonly used to loop a fixed number of times.

```python
for i in range(5):        # 0,1,2,3,4
    print(i)

for i in range(2, 10, 2): # 2,4,6,8 (start, stop, step)
    print(i)
```

sections.title: 🧮 enumerate()
sections.content:
Get both the index and the value while looping.

```python
for i, fruit in enumerate(["apple", "banana"]):
    print(i, fruit)   # 0 apple / 1 banana
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Assuming `range(5)` includes 5 — it stops right before the stop value.

questions.question: What does `range(5)` produce?
questions.explanation: range(stop) starts at 0 and excludes the stop value.

questions.question: What does `range(2, 8, 2)` produce?
questions.explanation: start, stop (exclusive), step: 2,4,6.

questions.question: `for x in "hi":` iterates over...
questions.explanation: Iterating a string yields one character at a time.

questions.question: What does `enumerate()` provide?
questions.explanation: enumerate() pairs each item with its position.

questions.question: Is the stop value in `range()` included?
questions.explanation: range excludes its stop value, like slicing.

questions.question: What does `for fruit in ['a','b']:` do?
questions.explanation: It iterates once per list element.

questions.question: range(10, 0, -1) counts...
questions.explanation: A negative step counts downward, stopping before 0.

questions.question: Which loop type is best for a known, fixed sequence of items?
questions.explanation: for loops are designed for iterating over sequences.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Use break to exit, continue to skip, and pass as a no-op placeholder.

sections.title: 🛑 break
sections.content:
Exits the loop entirely.

```python
for n in range(10):
    if n == 5:
        break
    print(n)   # prints 0,1,2,3,4
```

sections.title: ⏭️ continue
sections.content:
Skips the rest of the current iteration and moves to the next.

```python
for n in range(5):
    if n == 2:
        continue
    print(n)   # prints 0,1,3,4 (skips 2)
```

sections.title: 🕳️ pass
sections.content:
Does nothing — a placeholder where syntax requires a statement.

```python
for n in range(5):
    if n == 2:
        pass  # TODO: handle this later
    print(n)
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Confusing break (stops the loop) with continue (skips just this iteration).

questions.question: What does `continue` do?
questions.explanation: continue jumps back to the loop's condition/next item.

questions.question: What does `break` do?
questions.explanation: break stops the loop immediately.

questions.question: What is `pass` used for?
questions.explanation: pass lets you write an empty block without a syntax error.

questions.question: In `for n in range(5): if n==2: continue; print(n)`, what's skipped?
questions.explanation: continue skips just that one print call.

questions.question: Can pass appear in an empty function body?
questions.explanation: def f(): pass is a common valid stub.

questions.question: After `break` runs inside a for loop, execution continues...
options: At the top of the loop again
At the start of the program
questions.explanation: break exits to the code following the loop.

questions.question: Which statement would you use to stub out an unfinished if-branch?
questions.explanation: pass is the placeholder for 'nothing here yet'.

questions.question: Does `continue` exit the loop?
questions.explanation: continue moves to the next iteration, not out of the loop.
